records.our_prose: Brussels sprouts are a cool-season brassica grown for the small, cabbage-like buds that form in the leaf axils along a tall central stalk, harvested progressively from the bottom up. A long-season crop needing roughly 90 to 180 days, it is timed to mature in cool fall and winter weather: heat gives loose, bitter sprouts, while frost actually sweetens them, so the best sprouts come after the first hard frosts. It is one of the most cold-hardy garden vegetables, standing in the garden into early winter while temperatures hold above about 20°F.

records.our_prose: Brussels sprouts are long-season heavy feeders that need steady nitrogen to build the tall, leafy stalk that carries the crop. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the bed before planting, then side-dress with nitrogen about 4 and 8 weeks after transplanting. Ease off heavy nitrogen once sprouts begin forming, since late, lush growth encourages loose, leafy sprouts and draws aphids.

records.our_prose: In California's hot interior valleys, set out brussels sprouts transplants in mid-to-late summer so they mature in the cool fall and winter. Keep them watered through the late-summer heat while they get established, then harvest from the bottom of the stalk up through the cool months. Summer heat is the enemy of good sprouts, so do not plant for a summer harvest.

records.our_prose: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: brussels sprouts are a cool-season brassica that builds a leafy stalk in mild weather but sets firm, tight sprouts only when temperatures cool, roughly into the 60°F to 65°F range. Through the hot months the plant either stalls or makes loose, leafy, bitter sprouts, and cabbage aphid pressure peaks, so the crop is grown to mature in the cool season and the hottest months are left out of the planting calendar. On the southern California coast the mild winter is the growing season and midsummer is too warm for firm sprouts, so brussels sprouts are planted in fall for a winter-into-spring harvest and the hottest months are excluded. (UC Master Gardeners San Diego County; UC IPM)

records.our_prose: In cold regions, brussels sprouts are a single long-season crop. Start seeds indoors in spring, plant them out in late spring or early summer, and let them grow all summer; the sprouts form as fall cools and taste best after frost. Harvest from the bottom of the stalk up through fall and into early winter. Deep winter cold eventually ends the crop.

records.our_prose: In the Southeast, brussels sprouts are a fall and winter crop, not a summer one. Start seeds indoors in mid-summer and set transplants out in late summer or early fall once the worst heat eases. Harvest through the mild winter into spring; frost makes the sprouts sweeter. Skip the hot summer, when the plants grow poorly and aphids are bad. Note that brussels sprouts are a minor, somewhat challenging crop in the Deep South because the cool window is short.

records.our_prose: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: brussels sprouts are a cool-season brassica that builds a leafy stalk in mild weather but sets firm, tight sprouts only when temperatures cool, roughly into the 60°F to 65°F range. Through the hot months the plant either stalls or makes loose, leafy, bitter sprouts, and cabbage aphid pressure peaks, so the crop is grown to mature in the cool season and the hottest months are left out of the planting calendar. In the hot, arid Southwest the late-spring and early-summer heat excludes brussels sprouts, which are grown as a fall transplant crop for a late-fall and winter harvest. (NMSU Cooperative Extension)

records.source_context: The name Brussels comes from the city Brussels, Belgium, where the vegetable first became popular. Brussels sprouts are a cool season vegetable that can be grown both in the fall and early spring. They also take a long time to mature, which can make them a little bit of a challenge for the home gardener.

records.our_prose: Brussels sprouts take a long time to grow, so it is easiest to start them as transplants. Sow seeds indoors about 5 to 6 weeks before you plant out. In cold areas, plant out in late spring or early summer so they mature in fall. In warm areas, plant in late summer or fall for a winter crop. Let homegrown seedlings get used to the outdoors over a week before planting.
